history.q: In what year did Morocco regain its independence from France?
history.fact: France recognised Morocco's independence on 2 March 1956, and Spain gave up most of its northern protectorate a few weeks later.

history.q: Which European country established a protectorate over most of Morocco with the Treaty of Fez in 1912?
history.fact: Spain received a separate zone in the north, and the French moved the seat of government from Fez to Rabat.

history.q: In January 1943, which two Allied leaders met at the Casablanca Conference?
history.fact: Meeting in the Anfa suburb of Casablanca, they announced that the Allies would accept nothing less than the Axis powers' unconditional surrender.

history.q: In 1777 Morocco is often cited as the first country to recognise the independence of which new nation?
history.fact: The 1786 Moroccan-American Treaty of Friendship is the United States' oldest unbroken treaty, and Tangier hosted its first overseas diplomatic property.

history.q: The well-preserved ruins of Volubilis, near Meknes, are mainly the remains of a city of which ancient empire?
history.fact: Volubilis grew rich exporting olive oil, and many of its floor mosaics still lie in place where they were laid.

history.q: Which great medieval traveller was born in Tangier in 1304?
history.fact: Over about 30 years Ibn Battuta covered some 117,000 km across Africa, Asia and Europe, then dictated his travels, the Rihla, back in Morocco.

history.q: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa into Iberia in 711. Which landmark still bears his name?
history.fact: Gibraltar comes from the Arabic Jabal Tariq, meaning 'Tariq's mountain'.

history.q: The English name 'Morocco' comes from which Moroccan city?
history.fact: In Arabic the country is al-Maghrib, 'the place where the sun sets', while Persian speakers still call it Marakesh.

history.q: Allied troops landed near Casablanca in November 1942 as part of which operation?
history.fact: Torch was the first large American operation of the war against Germany's Axis in the European-African theatre, with landings in Morocco and Algeria.

history.q: Which dynasty has reigned in Morocco since the 17th century?
history.fact: The Alaouites came to power in the 1660s, and their dynasty has reigned without interruption ever since.

history.q: Idris I founded which dynasty in 788, whose rulers went on to establish the city of Fez?
history.fact: Fez grew from twin settlements on either bank of its river; today its medina is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a maze of some 9,000 alleys.

history.q: Which Berber dynasty founded Marrakesh around 1070?
history.fact: Under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the Almoravids ruled an empire that stretched from the Senegal River into Spain.

history.q: Sultan Mohammed V returned from exile in which year, paving the way to independence?
history.fact: French authorities had exiled him in 1953; Morocco's Independence Day on 18 November recalls the speech he gave after his return.

history.q: Which city was run as an international zone by several foreign powers from the 1920s until 1956?
history.fact: Interzone Tangier drew spies, bankers and writers, from Paul Bowles to William S. Burroughs, who wrote much of 'Naked Lunch' there.

history.q: Which city served as the capital of Spain's protectorate zone in northern Morocco?
history.fact: Tetouan's whitewashed medina, rebuilt by refugees from Andalusia in the late 15th century, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: Which Rif leader defeated a Spanish army at the Battle of Annual in 1921?
history.fact: Abd el-Krim proclaimed a Republic of the Rif, which held out until a joint French-Spanish campaign forced his surrender in 1926.

history.q: Which European king was killed at the Battle of Ksar el-Kebir, the 'Battle of the Three Kings', in 1578?
history.fact: Sebastian died without an heir, which led to Portugal's union with Spain in 1580, while the victory brought great prestige to Morocco's Ahmad al-Mansur.

history.q: Who founded the al-Qarawiyyin mosque and centre of learning in Fez in 859?
history.fact: Al-Qarawiyyin is often described as the world's oldest continuously operating educational institution.

history.q: In 1591 an army sent by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur crossed the Sahara and defeated which empire at Tondibi?
history.fact: The army, led by the Spanish-born commander Judar Pasha, carried firearms across the desert and went on to occupy Timbuktu and Gao.

history.q: Which Alaouite sultan, reigning for 55 years from 1672, made Meknes his imperial capital?
history.fact: He ringed Meknes with tens of kilometres of walls and monumental gates; the historic city is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: Whose landing at Tangier in 1905 triggered the First Moroccan Crisis?
history.fact: The crisis was settled at the Algeciras Conference of 1906, which confirmed French and Spanish influence in Morocco.

history.q: The arrival of which German gunboat at Agadir in 1911 sparked the Agadir Crisis?
history.fact: Germany eventually accepted a French protectorate over Morocco in return for a slice of French territory in Central Africa.

history.q: Juba II, the Roman client king of Mauretania, married the daughter of which famous queen?
history.fact: His wife, Cleopatra Selene, was the daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony; Juba himself was a scholar who wrote books in Greek.

history.q: Which Granada-born scholar, raised in Fez, wrote the 'Description of Africa' published in 1550?
history.fact: Born al-Hasan al-Wazzan, he was captured by corsairs and presented to Pope Leo X, whose name he took.

history.q: Which Atlantic city was the Portuguese fortress of Mazagan until 1769?
history.fact: Its vaulted Portuguese Cistern, lit by a single round opening in the roof, appears in Orson Welles's film 'Othello'.

technology.q: The vast Noor complex near Ouarzazate generates electricity from what?
technology.fact: Noor, Arabic for 'light', is among the world's largest concentrated solar power complexes, using mirrors to focus desert sunshine.

technology.q: Morocco holds the world's largest reserves of which mineral resource, a key ingredient of fertilisers?
technology.fact: Phosphorus is one of the three main crop nutrients, alongside nitrogen and potassium, so Moroccan rock helps feed farms around the world.

technology.q: In 2018 Morocco opened Africa's first high-speed railway, linking Tangier with which city?
technology.fact: The Al Boraq service, named after a winged steed of Islamic tradition, cut the Tangier-Casablanca journey from nearly five hours to about two.

technology.q: Since 1997, undersea power cables have linked Morocco's electricity grid with which country?
technology.fact: The cables beneath the Strait of Gibraltar are the only electricity link between Africa and Europe.

technology.q: Which oil is pressed from the kernels of a tree that grows wild almost only in southwestern Morocco?
technology.fact: Much of it is produced by women's cooperatives, and the argan forest region is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

technology.q: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, dated in 2017 to about 300,000 years old, are among the oldest known remains of which species?
technology.fact: The find pushed back our species' known origins by about 100,000 years and suggested Homo sapiens emerged across Africa, not in a single cradle.

technology.q: The Tissint meteorite, seen falling over southern Morocco in 2011, came from which world?
technology.fact: Witnessed falls of Martian meteorites are extremely rare, and Tissint's fresh fragments preserved traces of the Red Planet's chemistry.

technology.q: What has been processed for centuries in the dye pits of Fez's Chouara Tannery?
technology.fact: Hides are softened in vats of lime and pigeon droppings, then coloured with natural dyes such as poppy, indigo and henna.

technology.q: Greenhouses on the Souss plain near Agadir make Morocco one of Europe's main suppliers of which crop?
technology.fact: Mild winters in the Souss-Massa region let growers harvest from autumn to spring, when fields in northern Europe are cold.

technology.q: Which French carmaker opened a large factory near Tangier in 2012?
technology.fact: Linked by rail to the Tanger Med port, the plant exports most of the cars it builds, many of them Dacias.

technology.q: Morocco's state phosphate company, founded in 1920, is known by which initials?
technology.fact: Founded as the Office Chérifien des Phosphates, OCP is today one of the world's largest producers of phosphate and fertilisers.

technology.q: Which town in central Morocco grew up around the country's first big phosphate mine, opened in the 1920s?
technology.fact: Khouribga sits on one of the world's richest phosphate basins; a slurry pipeline now carries the ore to the coast at Jorf Lasfar.

technology.q: Which Córdoba-born philosopher and physician served the Almohad court and died in Marrakesh in 1198?
technology.fact: His commentaries on Aristotle were so influential in medieval Europe that he was known simply as 'the Commentator'.

technology.q: Moroccan-born scientist Rachid Yazami shared the 2014 Draper Prize for pioneering work on which technology?
technology.fact: In 1980 he showed that lithium could be reversibly stored in graphite, the basis of the anode in most lithium-ion batteries.

technology.q: What part of Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque can slide open to the sky?
technology.fact: Completed in 1993, the mosque stands partly over the Atlantic, and its prayer hall can hold around 25,000 worshippers.

technology.q: What are the khettaras of Morocco's Tafilalet region?
technology.fact: Like Persian qanats, these gently sloping tunnels carry groundwater by gravity to oasis fields, marked on the surface by lines of shafts.

technology.q: What top speed do Morocco's Al Boraq high-speed trains reach in regular service?
technology.fact: During a test run in 2017, one of the trains reached 357 km/h, a rail speed record for Africa.

technology.q: What type of bridge is the Mohammed VI Bridge, opened in 2016 across the Bou Regreg valley near Rabat?
technology.fact: Its two arch-shaped pylons echo traditional city gates, and it was billed as Africa's longest cable-stayed bridge when it opened.

technology.q: Which mathematician from Marrakesh (1256-1321) wrote the influential arithmetic manual 'Talkhis a'mal al-hisab'?
technology.fact: His concise summary of arithmetic was studied, copied and commented on across North Africa for centuries.

technology.q: Fez's Dar al-Magana, built in 1357 facing the Bou Inania Madrasa, housed what device?
technology.fact: A row of windows and brass bowls once marked the hours, but exactly how its long-lost mechanism worked is still debated.

technology.q: Morocco's Earth-observation satellite Mohammed VI-A was launched in 2017 from which spaceport?
technology.fact: It rode a European Vega rocket, and a twin satellite, Mohammed VI-B, followed from the same spaceport in 2018.

technology.q: Which southern coastal town hosts a 301 MW wind farm, opened in 2014 and among Africa's largest?
technology.fact: Its 131 turbines catch the steady trade winds blowing off the Atlantic near Cape Juby.

technology.q: Perforated shell beads at least 142,000 years old, reported in 2021, were found in which cave near Essaouira?
technology.fact: They are among the oldest known personal ornaments, hinting that early humans used jewellery to signal identity.

technology.q: A 2020 study of a Spinosaurus skeleton from Morocco's Kem Kem beds revealed what swimming adaptation?
technology.fact: The tall, flexible tail was strong evidence that this giant predator propelled itself through water like a crocodile.

technology.q: Which material stores heat at the Noor Ouarzazate solar plants so they can keep generating after sunset?
technology.fact: Sun-heated salt is kept in huge insulated tanks and later used to make steam, letting the plants supply power for hours after dark.

art.q: What is zellij, a hallmark of Moroccan palaces and fountains?
art.fact: Craftsmen chip each tiny piece by hand from glazed terracotta, then fit them together into intricate geometric stars.

art.q: Which fashion designer bought and restored Marrakesh's Jardin Majorelle with Pierre Bergé in 1980?
art.fact: The garden was created by painter Jacques Majorelle, whose vivid cobalt shade is now known as 'Majorelle blue'.

art.q: Where was the 1942 film 'Casablanca' almost entirely shot?
art.fact: Apart from scenes at a Los Angeles-area airport, it was made on Warner Bros. sound stages, and it went on to win the Oscar for Best Picture.

art.q: The mud-brick ksar of Aït Benhaddou has served as a location for which film?
art.fact: The UNESCO-listed fortified village has also appeared in 'Lawrence of Arabia' and 'Game of Thrones'.

art.q: Essaouira's big annual festival celebrates which spiritual music with sub-Saharan roots?
art.fact: Gnawa musicians play iron castanets called qraqeb, building hypnotic rhythms that can carry a ceremony through the night.

art.q: Which 12th-century minaret, about 77 m tall, dominates the skyline of Marrakesh?
art.fact: Its name comes from the booksellers, the kutubiyyin, who once traded at its foot.

art.q: Roughly how tall is the minaret of Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque, completed in 1993?
art.fact: At night a laser beam shines from its summit in the direction of Mecca.

art.q: What are babouches, sold by the thousand in Moroccan souks?
art.fact: Soft, heelless and easy to slip off at the door, classic men's babouches come in a bright saffron yellow.

art.q: Which American writer, who settled in Tangier, wrote the 1949 novel 'The Sheltering Sky'?
art.fact: Bowles lived in Tangier for more than 50 years and also made landmark field recordings of traditional Moroccan music.

art.q: Which French Romantic painter filled sketchbooks during a diplomatic mission to Morocco in 1832?
art.fact: Delacroix drew on these sketches for decades, in works such as 'Jewish Wedding in Morocco'.

art.q: Which painter created 'Window at Tangier' during stays in Morocco in 1912-13?
art.fact: Matisse's room at Tangier's Grand Hotel Villa de France, the view from which he painted, is preserved for visiting art lovers.

art.q: Fez's Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas, masterpieces of carved cedar and stucco, were built by which dynasty?
art.fact: Built in the 14th century, the Bou Inania is one of the few religious buildings in Morocco that non-Muslim visitors may enter.

art.q: Seville's Giralda tower began as a minaret built by which dynasty, which also raised Marrakesh's Koutoubia?
art.fact: The Giralda, the Koutoubia and Rabat's unfinished Hassan Tower are often called three sister towers.

art.q: Which Tangier author wrote the autobiographical novel 'For Bread Alone'?
art.fact: Paul Bowles's English translation appeared in 1973, almost a decade before the Arabic original was published.

art.q: Which Moroccan author won France's Prix Goncourt in 1987 for 'The Sacred Night'?
art.fact: 'The Sacred Night' continued the story begun in his earlier novel 'The Sand Child'.

art.q: Which 1956 Alfred Hitchcock thriller opens in Marrakesh?
choices: The Man Who Knew Too Much
art.fact: Starring James Stewart and Doris Day, it introduced the song 'Que Sera, Sera', which won the Oscar for Best Original Song.

art.q: Which Atlantic port is renowned as Morocco's capital of pottery?
art.fact: Safi's potters work in a hillside quarter called the Colline des Potiers, firing glazed ceramics in traditional kilns.

art.q: Which Saadian sultan built Marrakesh's El Badi Palace after the victory of 1578?
art.fact: Its name means 'the incomparable'; a century later Moulay Ismail stripped its marble and gold to adorn Meknes.

art.q: Which 1960s modernist art movement grew around Farid Belkahia, Mohamed Melehi and Mohamed Chabâa?
art.fact: Teaching at the city's fine-arts school, they drew on Amazigh motifs, crafts and calligraphy rather than European academic painting.

art.q: Orson Welles shot much of 'Othello', which won the top prize at Cannes in 1952, in which walled port?
art.fact: Essaouira, then known as Mogador, later named a seafront square after the director.

art.q: Rolling Stones guitarist Brian Jones recorded which group of musicians in a Rif village in 1968?
art.fact: The album came out in 1971 after Jones's death, and the musicians later played on the Rolling Stones' 'Continental Drift' (1989).

art.q: Which three-stringed bass lute is the central instrument of Gnawa music?
art.fact: Also called the sintir or hajhouj, it has a skin-covered body and is played by the maâlem, the master musician who leads the ceremony.

art.q: Which 1970s Casablanca group, often dubbed 'the Rolling Stones of Africa', transformed Moroccan popular music?
art.fact: Formed in Casablanca's Hay Mohammadi district, the band blended Gnawa rhythms, Sufi chants and sung poetry about everyday life.

art.q: Which director made 'Ali Zaoua' (2000), about street children in Casablanca?
art.fact: Ayouch cast children who really lived on Casablanca's streets, and the film became one of Morocco's best-known abroad.

art.q: Essaouira's woodworkers are famous for marquetry made from the burl of which fragrant local tree?
art.fact: The thuya's knotted root burl is polished to a rich swirling grain and often inlaid with lemonwood or mother-of-pearl.
